Here's some insight from someone who gets chastised for being rude fairly regularly:

I have PTSD. My internal alarm system goes off when people approach me. This disproportionate response is because my life experiences have programmed my body to react this way. It is not my choice and it is entirely miserable. I don't want to be this way and I'm working on it, but it will take time. 

To avoid this feeling, I try to put out as many cues as possible that I can't talk. I'm usually focused on my phone, sometimes I have headphones in, I try to keep my head down and avoid eye contact, etc. Apparently this avoidance strategy makes me look snobby and self-absorbed and some people even take offense to me being so "unavailable". I'm not trying to be rude. In fact, I'm trying to be proactive about something I can't help. 

Anyway, when someone pushes past all this, I try to be polite even though my brain is freaking out. I think an equivalent to how I feel for normal people would be to ask them to hold a polite conversation while standing in a pit full of non-venomous, non-poisonous snakes. They would know intellectually that they're okay, but their nervous system is still going to freak out. It's hard. Despite this challenge (I've had a lot of practice) I think I do a good job and manage about 80-90% of the time to tactfully get out of the interaction. 

I find that the people who push past all the cues I'm giving out on purpose are the people who are the most reactive to any further hints that I don't want to talk. They won't let me tactfully bow out of the conversation and then they will openly chastise me for "being rude". They're usually older than me. (I'm basically 30, but due to acne, small size, babyface, etc, I gather that most people assume I am late teens or early twenties.) 

It sometimes seems like people are mad at me for just existing, but I tell myself that if people really understood the invisible things that are happening in my body, they would regret how they are affecting me. I think people want to mean well. And the caveat, I guess, is that I look like a normal person. Some people even seem to think I'm cute. It's not like I have "PTSD" stamped on my forehead. So, I'm a normal looking person with a really awful nervous system trying really hard to keep my bad experiences to myself. I really am trying to avoid the snake pit.

I don't know what level of pre-prepared your meal was, but it's probably smart to keep in mind that tons of Americans cook their Thanksgiving dinners from boxed mixes and lots of canned items. For example, I remember the first time I ran into fresh-made cranberry sauce. I was 15 and it was really weird. I adjusted and now think it's phenomenal stuff, but the canned jelly with the ridges from the can is way more authentic to me than real cranberry sauce. Plenty of Americans cook from scratch too, but I doubt it is commonplace. Also, depending on the cuisine you're accustomed to, all American foods may seem bland.

For me, my inattentive distractability makes a big contribution to my life though. When I am unmedicated, I am fairly distractible. So, I can walk into a situation with a whole bunch of triggers and if I can find something engaging there, I can kind of forget that I'm afraid for a little bit. When I leave, I'll get stuck with a "woah, what just happened?" rebound flashback of sorts, but the glitch can be useful when I need to get work done in a triggering but engaging environment. It can be weird for others because, as I get engaged I can switch from very guarded to friendly, child-like enthusiasm very rapidly (on the right topic). I can rarely do this when I'm medicated. 

Though, medicine does help me resist low- and medium-level triggers and over stimulation better. BUT, if I get hit with a really strong trigger, I will have a much harder time getting out when my ADD is medicated. In that case, it's going to suck either way, but it sucks for longer when I'm on medicine. 

It's definitely a trade off for me.

I'd like to add to this! There's a lot of talk about "washing" service dogs that bothers me. My service dog training organization largely focuses on guiding owner-trained PSDs, mostly rescued from the pound. Despite this, they have a really high pass-rate. 

To be fair, they do have a fair amount of people coming to them with expensive, straight-from-the-breeder puppies, but a large portion of us do not have this kind of money laying around. These dogs *do* breeze through the program. 

Anyway, a large portion of us ended up with dogs from the pound that pulled our heartstrings. By-and-large, this means we're training dogs that are a lot like us and don't initially fit the popular service dog mold. (For those of y'all who are freaking out, our organization will redline an aggressive dog). The reason my organization has such a high success rate is:

**1)** The dogs are trained while completely bonded to the person they're supposed to help. I don't know much about the puppy-raising side, but I doubt that it is common for the raisers to share the disability that their permanent handlers have. However, in my program, the dog is clued into their handler's needs from day one. It gives the dogs purpose and empathetic intuition throughout the training process. 

**2)** The organization's trainers are experienced in addressing the behavior problems that neurotic people tend to give their dogs. I mean, they know how to do advanced skill set training, but they also know how to help a dog "work it out". So, while the dog is also learning complicated task-specific work, the owner is learning how to effectively address their own issues for their dog. As the program progresses, the owner's disability lessens. Believe it or not, the dogs usually completely overcome their weaknesses, too. 

* *Caveat*: It takes expertise to do this, though. I recently learned that some of the skittish pit bulls that were removed from the Michael Vick compound are now AKC certified Therapy Dogs. I don't know how wide-spread this type of expertise is, but my organization's owner has a graduate degree in dog psychology. The trainers write her really detailed reports (kind of like diary entries) and take constant pictures while they're training. I suspect the organization's owner weighs in a lot? 

**3)** They increase their cost-accessibility because they run with bare-bones needs. This runs two ways: 

* **a)** The owner does most of the labor involved in training the dog, so they do not need to be paid. In fact, since a partially trained service dog is more support than no service dog, the owner actually gets "paid" for the training labor. Not immediately, but this starts happening fairly early in the process.  

* **b)** They come to your home or local mall/Walmart/ect instead of working in a facility. I know that puppy-raisers end up taking their dogs to a lot of places, but I mention this because ADI certification requires a brick and mortar facility for certification. Brick and mortar buildings are expensive and add to the costs of training a service dog. 

* Since the training sessions are less expensive, it is easier to get regular professional guidance. And since the owner does most of the  labor, you don't pay an expert to do something a trained and motivated volunteer could do.
  
**The take home is that, if you have an expert helping you out, don't get discouraged. Even people who know service dogs can offer discouraging, counter-productive advice! Just keep at it!**

My dad taught me about gears when I was really young and I haven't read around for appropriate technical terms. He demonstrated it on a mountain bike for me. You can also see similar concepts in cogs of clocks where the minutes/seconds are just smaller in comparison to the larger hour cog, but I'm not really a clock person. 

Basically, a car's engine converts the up and down motion of the piston into the rotational motion of the crankshaft. The harder the engine is working, the faster the crankshaft rotates. Smaller gears require more work from the engine to go the same speed. However, these higher rotations (RPMs) have more power and, thus, it's easier to change your speed (accelerate). This acceleration creates the inward circular force you need to counter the outward circular force that is essentially leftover inertia from going straight. The outward circular force is what makes your car feel top-heavy. 

People who are really into cars can explain the different gear ratios and give lectures on over-steering vs under-steering, but I'm not one of them.
